clinicalPearls: Osteoarthritis of the facet (zygapophysial) joints causing axial, mechanical spinal pain
Pain is typically worse with extension, rotation, and standing, and often eased by flexion or sitting
Lumbar facet pain may refer to the buttock and posterior thigh but characteristically not below the knee
Localised paraspinal tenderness over the facets and pain on extension and rotation are suggestive but not specific
No clinical test reliably diagnoses facet-mediated pain, and imaging findings of facet hypertrophy and effusion correlate poorly with symptoms
Diagnostic medial branch blocks are the most specific way to implicate the facet joint
Management is conservative (physiotherapy, analgesia), and intra-articular or medial branch injections may help selected patients
Radiofrequency denervation of the medial branches can give medium-term relief when diagnostic blocks are positive
reference.pathophysiology: Facet joint syndrome refers to pain arising from the synovial zygapophysial joints of the spine. These joints, richly innervated by the medial branches of the dorsal rami, undergo osteoarthritic change (cartilage loss, capsular hypertrophy, osteophytosis, and effusion) as part of the degenerative cascade, frequently alongside disc degeneration. Mechanical loading in extension and rotation together with inflammation of the joint capsule stimulates nociceptors and produces axial pain. Facet hypertrophy can also contribute to lateral recess and foraminal narrowing.
additionalInvestigations: MRI or CT showing facet arthropathy, hypertrophy, and effusions
Plain radiographs for alignment and degenerative change
Diagnostic medial branch blocks or intra-articular facet injection to confirm the pain source
SPECT/CT to identify metabolically active painful facets in selected cases
Inflammatory screen if spondyloarthropathy is a consideration
redFlags: New neurological deficit or radicular symptoms
Constitutional symptoms suggesting infection or malignancy
Features of inflammatory back pain such as morning stiffness, night pain, and young age
reference.prognosis: Facet-mediated pain typically follows a fluctuating chronic course; many patients are managed conservatively, and those with confirmed facet pain often gain useful, though sometimes temporary, relief from injections or radiofrequency denervation.
pitfalls: Diagnosing facet syndrome on imaging alone given the poor correlation between imaging and symptoms
Neglecting a structured conservative programme before interventional procedures
Overlooking concurrent discogenic or sacroiliac pain sources
references: Bogduk: Clinical Anatomy of the Lumbar Spine and Sacrum
management: First-line conservative care with physiotherapy targeting core and paraspinal strengthening, posture and activity modification that avoids provocative extension and rotation
Simple analgesia with paracetamol and short courses of NSAIDs for symptomatic flares
Diagnostic medial branch blocks to confirm the facet joint as the pain source before intervention
Radiofrequency medial branch neurotomy for confirmed, recurrent facet-mediated pain
Intra-articular corticosteroid and local anaesthetic injection for symptomatic relief in selected cases
Weight management and correction of modifiable postural and occupational loading factors
Referral to a pain or spinal specialist for refractory pain, with escalation if red-flag or radicular neurological features emerge
